v3/u21/teach/listening/c1p1.title: Note completion: predict the form before the voice starts
v3/u21/teach/listening/c1p1.one_line: You can know the shape of every answer before you hear a word.

steps.say: This is a telephone enquiry and the task is note completion. Five gaps, one word or a number each, and they come in the order you hear them.
Before the recording starts you have time, and the only useful thing to do with it is predict the FORM of each answer. Not the word - the kind of word.
A family name will be spelled out. A grade will be letters. A month will be a month. A number of weeks will be a small number. You now know four of five shapes.
Why this matters: if you are listening for a month and you hear a month, you write it. If you are listening for anything at all, you hear everything and write nothing.
One warning for this recording. A speaker who spells a name is telling you the answer is the name - but they often say it once before spelling it. Write it, then check the letters.
And it is played once. If you miss one, leave it and move to the next gap. The commonest way to lose three marks is to spend the time hunting for one.

scene.caption: Five gaps, four shapes known in advance

parts.text: Note completion · ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER · in the order you hear them
the time before the recording is for predicting the FORM
a name (spelled)   ·   a grade (letters)   ·   a month   ·   a small number
listening for a KIND of word → you hear it   ·   listening for anything → you hear everything
said once, then spelled — write, then check
played once — leave a gap, keep moving

v3/u21/teach/listening/c1p2.title: A talk: short answer and the signposts that precede it
v3/u21/teach/listening/c1p2.one_line: A monologue tells you a list is coming. Count it.

steps.say: A single speaker talking to an audience. The structure is nearly always the same: a frame, then a numbered list, then a closing point.
The frame is the sentence that says how many things are coming. First, second, third. When you hear a number word at the start of a sentence, a point is beginning.
Short-answer questions in a talk almost always sit on those numbered points, in order. So number your page before the audio starts.
Watch for the speaker who says a thing and then corrects it. In a talk the correction is the answer, because the examiner chose that moment on purpose.
And keep your answers short. A short-answer question with a three-word limit does not want the speaker's whole sentence; it wants the noun they landed on.

parts.text: frame  →  first · second · third  →  closing point
a number word at the start of a sentence = a new point
number your page before the audio starts
when a speaker corrects themselves, the correction is the answer
answer with the noun they landed on, not the sentence

practice.instruction: Answer with ONE WORD describing the listening behaviour, not the content.

questions.stem: A speaker says 'First, the time.' What does that word signal?
questions.why: An ordinal at the start of a sentence opens a new numbered point, which is where short-answer questions sit.

questions.stem: A speaker gives a figure, pauses, then gives a different one. Which do you write?
questions.why: The correction is the answer; the examiner placed the first figure to catch a candidate who stops listening.

questions.stem: You miss question 16 entirely. What do you do next?
questions.why: The recording is played once and the questions run in order, so hunting for one lost answer costs the next two.

grounds: the task type and its rubric
ask.refuse: I will not give you the content of the talk before you have heard it. Ask about how to listen to it.

v3/u21/teach/listening/c2p2.title: Sentence completion: the grammar of the gap
v3/u21/teach/listening/c2p2.one_line: The sentence around the gap tells you what part of speech must fill it.

steps.say: Sentence completion looks like a memory test and is really a grammar test. The words around the gap decide what can go in it.
An article before the gap means a noun is coming. A preposition before it means a noun too. An adverb of degree means an adjective.
Do this in the preparation time and write the part of speech above each gap. Two seconds a gap, and it halves what you have to hold in your head.
Then the trap. The recording will paraphrase the sentence on your page. The words will not match; the meaning will. Listen for the idea, write the word you hear.
And check the sentence reads correctly afterwards. A gap-fill answer that makes the sentence ungrammatical is almost always the wrong word.

scene.caption: What can go in the gap

parts.text: sentence completion is a grammar test wearing a memory test's clothes
the ___ → a noun      ·      in/on/at ___ → a noun      ·      very ___ → an adjective
write the part of speech above each gap
the audio paraphrases — the meaning matches, the words do not
read the sentence back — if it is ungrammatical, it is wrong

practice.instruction: What part of speech must fill the gap? Write ONE WORD.

questions.stem: 'The school was asked to supply a ____________ .'  The gap needs a ____________.
questions.why: An indefinite article immediately before a gap can only be followed by a noun phrase.

questions.stem: 'Attainment rose very ____________ in the second year.'  The gap needs an ____________.
questions.why: 'very' modifies a gradable word and the slot follows a verb, so an adverb of degree fits.

questions.stem: 'The decision depends on the ____________ of the report.'  The gap needs a ____________.
questions.why: A preposition followed by 'the' can only introduce a noun.

grounds: the task type and its rubric

v3/u21/teach/listening/c2p3.title: Two people disagreeing: whose opinion does the question want?
v3/u21/teach/listening/c2p3.one_line: In a discussion, track the person as carefully as the point.

steps.say: Two speakers who disagree, and multiple choice. The question will name a person, and the wrong options are usually things the other person said.
So before you listen, underline the name in each question. That one mark turns half the distractors off.
Then listen for the moment of concession. In a disagreement both speakers agree about something first, and the question often sits on exactly that.
Beware agreement that is not agreement. 'I take that point, but' means the speaker is about to disagree, and the part after but is their view.
And never choose an option because you heard the words in it. In a discussion, hearing the words is the trap; the question is about who meant them.

scene.caption: Two voices, one question at a time

parts.text:
speaker A
holds a position

speaker B
holds another
underline the NAME in each question before the audio starts
the concession — what they both accept — is where questions sit
'I take that point, but …' = disagreement
hearing the words ≠ the right option

v3/u21/teach/listening/c3p4.title: A lecture: the sentence that tells you the answer is coming
v3/u21/teach/listening/c3p4.one_line: Academic speakers announce their points before they make them.

steps.say: Part 4 is a lecture: one voice, no interruption, and the hardest listening in the paper. It is also the most predictable, because academic speakers signpost.
Listen for the announcing sentence. 'What I want to do first is', 'the key distinction here is', 'and this is the part people find hardest'. Each one says: the next sentence matters.
The questions for a lecture run in order and spread evenly through it. If you are on question 42 and the speaker is clearly past it, write something and move on.
This lecture is about reading figures, so expect numbers you must not simply copy. A speaker who gives two numbers in a sentence is asking which one the question wants.
And note the qualifier. In an academic talk, 'tends to', 'on average' and 'in most cases' are not padding - they are often the difference between the right option and a near one.

parts.text: Part 4 · one voice · no interruption · questions in order
“what I want to do first…”   “the key distinction is…”   “the part people find hardest…”
past it? write something, move on
two numbers in a sentence = a choice
'tends to' · 'on average' · 'in most cases' — the qualifier is often the answer

practice.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.stem: A lecturer says 'the key distinction here is'. What should you do?

options.text: Write — the next sentence is likely to be an answer
Go back to the previous question

questions.why: An announcing sentence in a lecture is a signpost that the point being tested is about to be made.

wrongs.A: Signposted material is the opposite of background.
wrongs.C: Questions run in order, so going back costs the one that is arriving.

questions.stem: The speaker says gains 'tend to shrink'. An option says gains 'always disappear'. Is it right?

questions.why: The qualifier is what the option changes, and changing a qualifier changes the claim.

wrongs.C: The one you missed is already gone; what is at risk is the rest.

v3/u21/teach/listening/c4p4.title: Evidence in a lecture: claim, support, limit
v3/u21/teach/listening/c4p4.one_line: Research talks move in threes, and the limit is where the marks are.

steps.say: A lecture about evidence has a rhythm: a claim, the support for it, and then the limit on it. Three beats, over and over.
Most candidates hear the claim and the support and stop listening at the limit, because it sounds like a digression. It is not. It is usually the question.
The limit is announced by a small set of words: although, however, what this does not show, the difficulty is, that said. Write them on your page now.
The second habit worth having here is to separate what was measured from what it means. A speaker often gives you both, and the options test which is which.
And if two options both sound true, choose the one the speaker actually said rather than the one you believe. This is a listening test, not a knowledge test.

parts.text: claim  →  support  →  LIMIT
the limit sounds like a digression and is usually the question
although · however · what this does not show · the difficulty is · that said
what was MEASURED ≠ what it MEANS
choose what was said, not what is true

practice.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.stem: Which of these usually introduces the answer in an evidence lecture?
questions.why: The limit on a claim is the part examiners build questions on, and it is announced by phrases of that kind.

wrongs.A: An example supports a claim already made and rarely carries a new testable point.
wrongs.C: A back-reference repeats; it does not add the qualification the question wants.

questions.stem: Two options both sound true, but you only heard one of them. Which do you choose?
questions.why: The task tests what the speaker said; outside knowledge is not evidence in a listening paper.

wrongs.B: Answering from your own knowledge is the commonest way to lose a mark you had.
wrongs.C: Never leave a blank — an unanswered question cannot be right.

questions.stem: A speaker reports a finding and then says 'although the sample was small'. What is that?
questions.why: A qualification of how far the finding reaches is the third beat of the pattern.

wrongs.A: The claim is the finding itself, which came first.
wrongs.B: Support is the evidence for the claim, not the caution about it.

grounds: the task type and its rubric

v3/u21/teach/listening/c5p4.title: Mixed tasks in one recording: switch cleanly
v3/u21/teach/listening/c5p4.one_line: When the task type changes mid-recording, the way you listen must change with it.

steps.say: This recording carries three task types at once - short answer, multiple choice and matching. That is normal in the real paper and it is the thing least practised.
Each type wants a different kind of attention. Short answer wants a noun. Multiple choice wants a comparison. Matching wants a person or a category.
So in the preparation time, mark where the type changes. A line across your page is enough. You are telling yourself when to switch.
The commonest loss here is carrying the wrong attention across the line - still hunting for a single word while the task has become a comparison.
And the second commonest: answering a matching question with a word from the recording instead of a letter from the list. Check the form of what you wrote.

parts.text: short answer  |  multiple choice  |  matching
a noun   ·   a comparison   ·   a person or category
draw a line where the type changes
the loss: the wrong attention, carried across
check the FORM of your answer — a letter where a letter is wanted

questions.why: A line where the task type changes tells you when to switch how you are listening.

v3/u21/teach/speaking/s1.title: The 2-to-5 shape, and where the stress lands
v3/u21/teach/speaking/s1.one_line: Part 1 answers are two sentences. Part 3 answers are five, with a concession.

quotes: In a long answer the strong stress lands once a sentence, on the word carrying the point.

steps.say: Speaking is the part of the paper most candidates practise least and worry about most. The series gives it a shape, and the shape is the whole technique.
Part 1 is two sentences. An answer, and a reason. Not one - one sounds like you have nothing to say. Not six - six sounds rehearsed.
Part 3 is four or five. A position, a reason, an example, and then a concession: the thing somebody who disagreed with you would say.
The concession is what moves a band. It shows you can hold two ideas at once, which is exactly what Fluency and Coherence is about at band 7.
Now the sound of it. The book's own rule: in a long answer the strong stress lands once a sentence, on the word carrying the point.
steps.anchor: In a long answer the strong stress lands once a sentence, on the word carrying the point.

steps.say: So practise one sentence at a time, deciding which single word carries it. Candidates who stress everything sound flat, and flat reads as uncertain.
And for Part 2, the card's bullets are the plan. Take them in order, give each roughly equal time, and you will fill two minutes without hurrying.

scene.caption: The shape of a spoken answer

parts.text: Part 1 · short answers    Part 2 · the long turn    Part 3 · the discussion

PART 1 — two sentences
answer + reason

PART 3 — four or five
position · reason · example
…and a concession — what somebody who disagreed would say
one strong stress a sentence, on the word carrying the point
stress everything → flat → reads as uncertain
Part 2: four bullets, in order, equal weight — and two minutes fills itself

v3/u21/teach/writing/w1.title: Two claims in one prompt: separate them before you plan
v3/u21/teach/writing/w1.one_line: Most Task 2 prompts hide two claims. Agreeing with one is not agreeing with both.

quotes: If the problem is scale, the policy conclusion is to stop. If the problem is dilution, the conclusion is to deliver fewer children the full programme, which is politically much harder,

steps.say: The commonest Task 2 failure is not bad English. It is answering a question the prompt did not ask, because the prompt contained two claims and the candidate saw one.
So before you plan, split it. Write the two claims as two separate sentences on your page. Now you can agree with one and disagree with the other, which is usually the honest position.
This unit's own reading does exactly that. The passage separates a problem of scale from a problem of dilution, and shows they point to opposite policies.
steps.anchor: If the problem is scale, the policy conclusion is to stop. If the problem is dilution, the conclusion is to deliver fewer children the full programme, which is politically much harder,

steps.say: Your opening paragraph should do the separating. Three sentences: here is claim one, here is claim two, and here is which of them I accept.
Then every body paragraph knows which claim it belongs to. That single move is most of Coherence and Cohesion, and it costs you thirty seconds at the start.
And concede generously before you disagree. An essay that has first agreed properly is far stronger than one that concedes a little and grudgingly.

scene.caption: Split the prompt before you plan

parts.text: one prompt, two claims hiding inside it

claim 1
written out on its own

claim 2
written out on its own
the passage does it: a problem of scale ≠ a problem of dilution
opening = claim 1 · claim 2 · which I accept
every paragraph knows which claim it serves
concede generously, then disagree — grudging agreement reads as reluctance

v3/u21/teach/grammar/g1.title: Asking politely: the indirect question
v3/u21/teach/grammar/g1.one_line: A direct question in a formal letter sounds abrupt. A vague one gets a vague answer.

steps.say: This unit's grammar is one pattern with one job: asking a precise question without sounding blunt. It is the pattern a formal letter runs on.
A direct question - Am I still being considered? - is clear and abrupt. In a letter it reads as a demand.
The indirect form wraps it: I would be grateful if you could tell me whether I am still being considered. Same question, no demand.
Notice two things the wrapping does to the grammar. The word order goes back to normal - I am, not am I - and a yes-no question needs whether or if.
The trap is over-wrapping. Three polite layers make a sentence nobody can answer. One opener, then the question, straight.
And stay precise. Please let me know what is happening is polite and useless. Ask for the thing you actually want to be told.

scene.caption: Direct → indirect, without losing the question

parts.text: precise and polite at the same time
Am I still being considered?

I would be grateful if you could tell me
whether I am still being considered.
word order returns to normal   ·   a yes-no question takes whether / if
three polite layers = unanswerable
“let me know what is happening” asks for nothing

v3/u21/teach/reading/p1.title: Reading an offer: every if is a question
v3/u21/teach/reading/p1.one_line: A page of conditions is a list of questions in disguise.

sources.skill_box: SKILL  ·  An offer with conditions is a list of questions
quotes: The standard offer for this course is BBB at A level, or an equivalent qualification.
We make contextual offers, normally one grade below the standard offer, to applicants who meet at least one of our contextual criteria.
A contextual offer is made automatically.
An offer is only withdrawn where the shortfall is substantial or where a required subject has not been passed.

steps.say: This is a university offer page. Before you read a word of it, notice what kind of text it is: it sets out conditions, and conditions are questions waiting to be asked.
The first paragraph gives the baseline. One offer, three grades. Everything after this is a change to that baseline, so hold it.
steps.anchor: The standard offer for this course is BBB at A level, or an equivalent qualification.

steps.say: Here is the first change. A contextual offer is lower - one grade, not two - and it is given to people who meet at least one criterion. Not all of them. One.
steps.anchor: We make contextual offers, normally one grade below the standard offer, to applicants who meet at least one of our contextual criteria.

steps.say: Now the sentence a careless reader skips. It is made automatically. You do not ask. Three of the five questions on this page turn on small words like that one.
steps.anchor: A contextual offer is made automatically.

steps.say: The last paragraph is the one with the word if in it, and that is where the conditions live. Narrowly miss, and you are still considered. Miss badly, or fail a required subject, and the offer goes.
steps.anchor: An offer is only withdrawn where the shortfall is substantial or where a required subject has not been passed.

steps.say: So the page is a ladder: a standard offer, a lower one for some people, given without asking, and withdrawn only in two named cases. Four facts. Five questions.

scene.caption: The offer, as a ladder of conditions

given automatically — you do not apply

v3/u21/teach/reading/p2.title: A process text: follow the application, not the sentences
v3/u21/teach/reading/p2.one_line: When a text describes a process, draw the process.

quotes: An application missing a reference or a predicted grade is held, and the applicant is contacted;
Complete applications are read by two assessors working independently.
Where the two assessors disagree by more than three points, the application goes to a third reader, whose decision is final.
Decisions are released on a single date for all applicants, which is why an early application does not receive an early answer.

steps.say: This passage describes a journey, and the questions follow the journey. So read it as a chain of stages, not as four paragraphs.
Stage one: the application arrives and is checked for completeness. Notice the careful word - an incomplete one is held, not rejected. It stops; it does not die.
steps.anchor: An application missing a reference or a predicted grade is held, and the applicant is contacted;

steps.say: Stage two: two assessors read it independently, each giving two scores. The word independently is doing work - they cannot see each other.
steps.anchor: Complete applications are read by two assessors working independently.

steps.say: Stage three happens only sometimes. If the two disagree by more than three points, a third reader decides, and that decision is final.
steps.anchor: Where the two assessors disagree by more than three points, the application goes to a third reader, whose decision is final.

steps.say: Stage four: everyone hears on one date. This is why applying early buys you nothing, which the passage says outright.
steps.anchor: Decisions are released on a single date for all applicants, which is why an early application does not receive an early answer.

steps.say: Four stages, one of them conditional. Draw that chain in the margin and every completion question has a place to sit.

two assessors
independently

third reader
if they differ by >3

one decision
date

incomplete → held, applicant contacted

v3/u21/teach/reading/p3.title: Four people, four positions: matching without re-reading
v3/u21/teach/reading/p3.one_line: Give each speaker one word before you look at the questions.

quotes: I chose the course because of the city, and I would say that out loud to anybody who asked.
I picked by employment figures and I now think that was a mistake.
Nobody in my family had been, so I applied to the one I had heard of.
I went to an open day at a place I had already decided against and changed my mind within an hour.

steps.say: Matching questions punish re-reading. Four people, six questions - if you go back to the text for each one, you read the passage six times.
So do this first. Read each person once and give them one word in the margin. Teodora: city.
steps.anchor: I chose the course because of the city, and I would say that out loud to anybody who asked.

steps.say: Nnamdi: numbers. And he regrets the method, not the place - that distinction is worth a mark later.
steps.anchor: I picked by employment figures and I now think that was a mistake.

steps.say: Isolde: no family. She applied to the only one she had heard of, and a teacher showed her the other forty.
steps.anchor: Nobody in my family had been, so I applied to the one I had heard of.

steps.say: Pavel: the visit. He changed his mind in an hour, and it was the students who did it.
steps.anchor: I went to an open day at a place I had already decided against and changed my mind within an hour.

steps.say: Four words - city, numbers, no family, visit. Now the questions are a lookup, not a search. That is the whole technique.

v3/u21/teach/reading/p4.title: A chart has a job, and so does its caption
v3/u21/teach/reading/p4.one_line: Read the numbers, then read what the writer says the numbers cannot do.

quotes: The chart shows median earnings five years after graduation, by subject group and by sex.
The gap between the sexes is present in every subject shown and is widest in economics, at seven thousand.
What a chart of this kind cannot show is what the same people would have earned without the degree.
A chart published next year describes a different cohort, and the subject order has in fact changed twice in the past fifteen years, with engineering rising and law falling.

steps.say: This passage has two halves and the questions come from both. The first half reads the chart. The second half argues about what the chart cannot tell you.
The chart itself: median earnings, five years out, by subject and by sex. Medicine at the top, creative arts at the bottom.
steps.anchor: The chart shows median earnings five years after graduation, by subject group and by sex.

steps.say: The gap between men and women is in every subject. Widest in economics at seven thousand, narrowest in creative arts. Watch for which figure a question wants.
steps.anchor: The gap between the sexes is present in every subject shown and is widest in economics, at seven thousand.

steps.say: Now the turn. The writer says the chart cannot show what those people would have earned without the degree. Part of medicine's figure is the students, not the teaching.
steps.anchor: What a chart of this kind cannot show is what the same people would have earned without the degree.

steps.say: And the second limit: this is one cohort in one labour market. Next year's chart describes different people - and the subject order has already changed twice in fifteen years.
steps.anchor: A chart published next year describes a different cohort, and the subject order has in fact changed twice in the past fifteen years, with engineering rising and law falling.

steps.say: So when a question asks what the chart shows, answer from the first half. When it asks what it proves, answer from the second. Most lost marks here are answers from the wrong half.

v3/u21/teach/reading/p5.title: A 732-word argument: find the turn in every paragraph
v3/u21/teach/reading/p5.one_line: Long passages are not harder. They are longer. Work paragraph by paragraph.

quotes: Most public argument about educational inequality concerns schools, and most of the gap that argument is about exists before a child has attended one.
What predicts a child's early language is not income itself but the quantity and kind of talk directed at them.
Fade-out is often reported as failure and that reading is too quick.
They predict later results robustly, whatever they are measuring.

steps.say: Seven hundred and thirty-two words, eleven paragraphs, seven questions. This is exam length. The method does not change - it just runs longer.
Paragraph one states the whole argument in one sentence: the gap people blame schools for already exists before school. Everything after this defends or qualifies that.
steps.anchor: Most public argument about educational inequality concerns schools, and most of the gap that argument is about exists before a child has attended one.

steps.say: The middle paragraphs make a distinction, and distinctions earn marks. It is not income that predicts language. It is the amount and kind of talk aimed at the child.
steps.anchor: What predicts a child's early language is not income itself but the quantity and kind of talk directed at them.

steps.say: Then the complication. Programmes work, and the gains shrink. The writer gives that shrinking a name - fade-out - and immediately says the obvious reading of it is too quick.
steps.anchor: Fade-out is often reported as failure and that reading is too quick.

steps.say: Notice what the writer never says. They never say early differences do not matter. They say the differences predict later results robustly, whatever they measure.
steps.anchor: They predict later results robustly, whatever they are measuring.

steps.say: That is where Yes, No and Not Given questions live on this passage. The writer qualifies almost everything, so a statement that sounds too flat is usually No.
One label per paragraph, two words each. Thesis. Vocabulary. Talk. What can be done. Fade-out. Too quick. Practised, not skill. And the questions become a lookup.

v3/u21/teach/reading/p6.title: Three programmes: when a comparison is the argument
v3/u21/teach/reading/p6.one_line: The writer sets up three cases so the difference between them can do the work.

quotes: The first was small, intensive and expensive: a few dozen children, daily sessions, trained staff, home visits.
The second was the same idea at national scale.
The intensive arm reproduced roughly two thirds of the original effect.
If the problem is scale, the policy conclusion is to stop. If the problem is dilution, the conclusion is to deliver fewer children the full programme, which is politically much harder,

steps.say: Three programmes, and they are not three examples. They are an argument. Each one exists to make the next one mean something.
The first: small, intensive, expensive. Daily sessions, trained staff, home visits, a few dozen children. These are the famous results.
steps.anchor: The first was small, intensive and expensive: a few dozen children, daily sessions, trained staff, home visits.

steps.say: The second: the same idea nationally. Thousands of settings, existing staff, an hour instead of a morning. The gains were much smaller.
steps.anchor: The second was the same idea at national scale.

steps.say: The third exists to explain the distance between the other two. It ran both models side by side in one city, and the intensive arm reproduced about two thirds of the effect.
steps.anchor: The intensive arm reproduced roughly two thirds of the original effect.

steps.say: Here is the sentence the whole passage was built to reach. Scale and dilution are different problems, and they point to opposite policies.
steps.anchor: If the problem is scale, the policy conclusion is to stop. If the problem is dilution, the conclusion is to deliver fewer children the full programme, which is politically much harder,

steps.say: When a passage compares three things, find the sentence that says why the comparison was made. It is usually the answer to the hardest question.
